# Preface {.unnumbered}

We came to the same conclusion from opposite directions.

Jesse was in his office when a developer who had been with him for years put in his notice. Sitting there, he realized he'd just lost something he couldn't replace — not just the person, but their *knowledge*. Every system the developer understood, every shortcut he'd built, every decision embedded in the codebase: walking out the door in a banker's box. Jesse had paid for years of that climb. And then the chute opened. That's when he understood his business was a game of "Chutes and Ladders:" he paid for the ladder and absorbed the cost of the chute. It was awful. And it had nothing to do with AI — AI was barely accessible technology at the time.

What that moment gave Jesse was something more foundational: he understood that knowledge in an organization is not ephemeral. It is an asset. And he had been treating it like air — always there until it wasn't. That realization started a years-long effort to treat knowledge as a first-class citizen. He built knowledge management systems. He trained the team to think about documentation, institutional memory, and structured information as real infrastructure — not an afterthought. When AI entered the mainstream, he was ready. The architecture was already in place. The practices were already habits. Combined with the discipline of running on EOS and the technical fluency of a software team, he had the raw ingredients for something that has since evolved into the system this book teaches.

In 2022, Julie was Global CHRO at a global food safety company when it completed the acquisition of a major division from a Fortune 500 company. Overnight, the organization expanded across 44 countries. The challenge wasn't technology. It was that the work — who owned what, how decisions moved, what knowledge lived where — had never been explicitly designed in either company before the acquisition. It lived in people's heads. When Julie asked leadership teams to describe their operating model, they described their org chart. Those aren't the same thing. The org chart names the boxes. The operating model names how work actually moves through those boxes.

Both stories point to the same gap. Before we can talk about AI, we need to say something most people haven't been told: AI is a new kind of worker. Not a chatbot you query — a worker you assign. It takes a task, produces an output, hands it off. When AI arrives inside your company, it arrives the same way a new employee does: looking for a seat, a scope, a set of handoffs. The problem is that the work was never explicitly designed in the first place. There's no seat for AI to occupy — for the same reason there was no seat for the developer's knowledge once he walked out, and no seat for a coherent operating model once the acquisition closed. That is why this book exists.

This book is about the design work — the operating design — that has to happen before any tool gets deployed. If you've bought tools and seen no return, this is why. If you want to know exactly what to do instead, read on.

What you will leave with is a six-step Sequence — Signal, Source, Design, Build, Deliver, Compound — and the sprint structure to run it. You can pick this book up and run the framework yourself.

When the design is right, 5:30 arrives and everything that needed to get done is done. You close the laptop and go home.

Your company is not just a business. It is a container for information — mediated by humans and, increasingly, by AI agents. The software you run, the databases you maintain, the documents your team creates — those are the neurons. The people who manage them are the operators. We are sitting at the precipice of one of the biggest changes in how work happens most of us will live through, and most of us already lived through the advent of the internet. This one is different. It changes not just how we operate, but the future of work itself — the future of teams, and the relationship humans have with machines that can think.

Jesse has spent his career at the intersection of technology and operations, from enterprise software to startup builds, developing AI systems inside real companies before teaching them to anyone else. He's also faculty at Michigan State University. Julie spent twenty years as a practitioner and executive in human capital and org design, most recently as Global CHRO at a global food safety company, where she led HR integration across a 44-country acquisition; prior to that, VP-level HR leadership at a global automotive supplier and earlier roles at a large furniture company and a precision manufacturer. Between the two of us: AI isn't a technology problem. It's a problem of how the work is set up. Fix the design before you deploy the tool. Design Before Deploy. Hence: co-intelligent co-operation.
